name: Spain
eraRationale: Six dated thresholds trace the peninsula’s course from pre‑Roman coastal colonisation through Romanisation, the long Muslim period, nineteenth‑century upheaval, civil war, and a peaceful democratic transition, as recorded in the cited sources.

moments.factText: c. 1,100–206 BC: the Iberian coast saw Phoenician, Greek and Carthaginian colonisation before Roman conquest.
moments.sourceRef: History of Spain Timeline - Globelink Blog
moments.narrativeCopy: Along the Iberian coast, Phoenician, Greek, and Carthaginian colonisation takes hold, a shoreline prelude to the coming Roman conquest.
moments.visualBrief: Coastal maps of the Iberian Peninsula; weathered stone foundations near shorelines; simple markers denoting Phoenician, Greek, and Carthaginian colonies along the coast.

moments.factText: From 206 BC to the 5th century AD, Rome conquered the peninsula, Romanised it, and introduced Latin, law, infrastructure and Christianity.
moments.sourceRef: History of Spain Timeline - Globelink Blog
moments.narrativeCopy: Across these centuries, Rome conquers the peninsula and Romanises it, introducing Latin, law, infrastructure, and Christianity.
moments.visualBrief: A provincial map labeled Hispania, dated 206 BC–5th century AD; robust stone infrastructure and civic architecture; orderly road tracings across the peninsula.

moments.factText: 711–1492: Muslim Spain (al‑Andalus) lasted more than 700 years and was divided into the Emirate, the Caliphate and the Taifa kingdoms.
moments.sourceRef: History of Spain Timeline - Globelink Blog
moments.narrativeCopy: For more than seven centuries, al‑Andalus endures, unfolding in the phases of the Emirate, the Caliphate, and the Taifa kingdoms.
moments.visualBrief: Period maps of the Iberian Peninsula marked 711–1492; courtyards and city walls from Islamic‑period Spain; architectural details rendered in stone and plaster.

moments.factText: In 1808 Napoleon defeated the Spanish army and replaced the king; after Napoleon’s defeat, Ferdinand VII restored the throne, followed by political instability and loss of colonies.
moments.sourceRef: History of Spain Timeline - Globelink Blog
moments.narrativeCopy: Upheaval breaks in 1808 as Napoleon defeats the Spanish army and replaces the king; after his defeat, Ferdinand VII restores the throne, and the era is marked by political instability and loss of colonies.
moments.visualBrief: Nineteenth‑century maps of the peninsula dated 1808–1874; fortress walls and artillery emplacements; official decrees and seals on aged paper.

moments.factText: 1936–1939: conflict between Republican and Nationalist forces.
moments.narrativeCopy: The peninsula divides into opposing camps as Republican and Nationalist forces wage a war from 1936 to 1939.
moments.visualBrief: Topographic maps of Spain annotated 1936–1939; field fortifications, sandbag lines, and neutral‑toned military textiles; urban street barricade remnants.

moments.factText: After 1975, Spain saw a peaceful transition, the 1978 constitution, EU membership in 1986, and modern democratic status.
moments.narrativeCopy: After 1975, a peaceful transition unfolds: the 1978 constitution is adopted; in 1986, membership in the European Union follows; Spain stands as a modern democracy.
moments.visualBrief: Facsimiles of the 1978 constitution; contemporary governmental building facades; a 1986 map of the European Union highlighting Spain.
